Learning Objectives
Discuss the osseous and soft-tissue anatomy relevant to the management of tibial plateau
fractures.
Perform an appropriate physical examination and interpret imaging studies in patients with a
tibial plateau fracture.
Describe the surgical management of tibial plateau fractures, including surgical approaches,
reduction techniques, and internal fixation strategies.
Review clinical outcomes and potential complications after the management of tibial plateau
fractures.

Tibial plateau fractures involve the joint surface of the proximal tibia that articulates with the
distal femur; they account for approximately 1% of all fractures.1
Similar to other periarticular fractures, tibial fractures typically occur in young patients who
sustain a high-energy mechanism of injury or in older patients who sustain a low-energy
mechanism of injury.
Tibial plateau fractures resulting from high-energy mechanisms of injury often are associated
with substantial soft-tissue injury and comminuted fracture patterns.2
Approximately 55% to 70% of fractures involve only the lateral tibial plateau, 10% to 23%
involve only the medial plateau, and 10% to 30% are bicondylar.3
Anatomy
Osteology
Proximal tibia anatomic alignment is a mean of 3° of varus, and the lateral plateau is stationed
more proximal than the medial plateau.
The medial plateau is larger and concave, and the lateral plateau is smaller and convex.
The medial plateau has a 10o posterior slope, and the lateral plateau has a 7° posterior slope.

Osteology
An understanding of the typical proximal tibia osseous relationships in an uninjured
state is critical for surgical and nonsurgical management of tibial plateau fractures. The
proximal tibia comprises the medial tibial plateau and lateral tibial plateau, each of
which can be subdivided into anterior and posterior components. Because of the
differences in size and morphology of the plateaus, the medial plateau bears
approximately 60% of the mechanical load of the knee.4
The femoral-tibial articulation of the knee has a mean coronal alignment 6o of valgus
resulting from 9o of anatomic valgus of the distal femur and 3o of anatomic varus of the
proximal tibia. The proximal tibia has a mean posterior slope of 9o.5 In managing tibial
plateau fractures the goal is to restore proper coronal and sagittal alignment and the
condylar heights and widths. Osseous anatomy varies, with the medial proximal tibia
angle ranging from 85o to 90o and the posterior proximal tibia angle ranging from 77o to

2/31

84o.5 Subtle variations exist among patients, and AP and lateral fluoroscopic images of
the contralateral uninjured knee aid in evaluation and restoration of articular and
proximal tibia alignment.
Neurovascular Structures
The popliteal artery passes through the popliteal fossa posterior to the posterior cruciate
ligament and branches into the inferior medial and lateral geniculate arteries near the
proximal tibia articular surface.
The popliteal artery terminally bifurcates into the anterior and posterior tibial arteries, with the
posterior tibial artery then branching into the peroneal artery.
The common peroneal nerve is posterior to the biceps femoris at the knee joint and then
travels around the fibular neck before dividing into the superficial and deep peroneal nerves.
The tibial nerve runs between the two heads of the gastrocnemius and into the deep posterior
compartment.
The saphenous nerve is superficial to the sartorius fascia in the proximal leg.

Neurovascular Structures
Patients with a tibial plateau fracture may have injuries to the surrounding
neurovascular structures. The incidence of vascular injury increases with fracture-
dislocation injury patterns.6,7 Safe development of the surgical approach around the
proximal tibia requires intimate knowledge of the nearby neurovascular structures.
Soft-Tissue Structures
The lateral meniscus, circular in shape, has no attachment to the lateral collateral ligament
and bears approximately 90% of the lateral joint load.8
The medial meniscus is C shaped, is intimately attached to the medial collateral ligament, and
bears approximately 50% of the medial joint load.8
The anterior and posterior cruciate ligaments insert onto the tibial spines.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:34 AM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004097
3/31

The medial collateral ligament, which attaches to the medial epicondyle of the femur and to
the medial condyle of the tibia, resists valgus forces.
The lateral collateral ligament, which attaches to the lateral epicondyle of the femur and to the
fibular head, resists varus forces.
The patellar ligament inserts on the tibial tubercle, which is located approximately 3 cm distal
to the articular surface.

Soft-Tissue Structures
Surgical management of tibial plateau fractures involves not only reduction and fixation
of the fractures but also recognition and possible management of the soft-tissue
structures of the knee. The most common soft-tissue injury associated with tibial plateau
fractures involves the menisci, with the lateral meniscus more commonly involved than
the medial meniscus.9 Approximately 60% of patients with a tibial plateau fracture have
tears to the lateral meniscus, most commonly involving separation of the peripheral
meniscus from the capsule.10 The medial collateral ligament is the most commonly
injured ligament, with complete rupture occurring in approximately 28% of patients with
a tibial plateau fracture.10 The higher incidence of lateral meniscus tears and medial
collateral ligament injury parallels the most common fracture pattern of a lateral tibial
plateau fracture with articular depression.11
Musculature
The iliotibial band attaches to the Gerdy tubercle on the anterolateral surface of the proximal
tibia and blends into the fascia of the proximal anterior leg compartment.
The tendon insertions of the sartorius, gracilis, and semitendinosus muscles attach to the
posteromedial surface of the proximal tibia.
The soleus muscle originates from the posterior aspect of the proximal tibia, and the
gastrocnemius originates from the posterior distal femur.
The popliteus travels obliquely across the posterior knee and inserts on the medial aspect of
the posterior proximal tibia.

Mechanism of Injury
Fracture pattern and displacement are dictated by the direction and magnitude of the forces
that injure the knee and by the position of the knee on impact.
Tibial plateau fractures often result from axial forces with the addition of an angular moment,
mostly commonly a valgus moment.12
Shearing forces involved with knee fracture-dislocations may be associated with higher risk of
injuries to the neurovascular structures6 and to ligaments and menisci.
Evaluation
Patient History and Physical Examination
The initial evaluation of tibial plateau fractures begins with a thorough patient history and
physical examination.
Important aspects of the patient history include age, mechanism of injury, associated injuries,
medical conditions, activity level, and preexisting knee symptoms.
A focused physical examination begins with inspection of the overlying soft tissues, followed
by a detailed neurovascular examination.
Initial and serial assessments for signs and symptoms of compartment syndrome should be
performed.

Patient History and Physical Examination
A detailed patient history and physical examination are important first steps in the
treatment of patients with a tibial plateau fracture. Certain factors from the patient
history may help dictate surgical versus nonsurgical management. The physical
examination should focus first on inspection for open wounds or other soft-tissue
injuries and noting any gross deformities around the knee (Figure 1). The status of the
soft tissues often will dictate early treatment of these patients and may substantially
affect outcomes. A vascular examination should start with palpation of the dorsalis pedis
and posterior tibial pulses. If pulses are not palpable, a Doppler device should be used to
detect signals of arterial flow. If pulses are not palpable and a Doppler device does not
detect any signals or if asymmetry of pulses is present between the injured and injured

0.9, additional angiography should be performed and/or vascular consultation should be
obtained. If neurologic examination reveals decreased sensation or motor weakness,

Figure 1 Clinical photograph shows soft-tissue injury in a lower extremity with a tibial
plateau fracture. (Courtesy of Stephen J. Warner, MD, PhD, Houston, TX.)
Imaging Studies
The initial evaluation should include AP and lateral radiographs of the knee.
Radiographs of the tibia, including the ankle, and of the femur, including the hip, also should
be obtained.
CT of the knee should be performed to better evaluate the fracture fragments and the injury
pattern.
CT often is performed after provisional external fixation and ligamentotaxis has been achieved
(Figure 2).

Figure 2 Images of a knee with a tibial plateau fracture. Preoperative AP (A) and lateral (B)
radiographs demonstrate the fracture. AP (C) and lateral (D) fluoroscopic images show
improved alignment after external fixation. (Courtesy of Stephen J. Warner, MD, PhD, Houston,
TX.)
MRI may be valuable in the acute setting with specific fracture patterns to evaluate for
associated soft-tissue injuries.

Imaging Studies
Initial injury radiographs are important for assessing the fracture characteristics and
displacement patterns in the coronal and sagittal planes, which may aid in planning
reduction and fixation strategies. The joints both above (hip) and below (ankle) the tibia
also should be assessed radiographically. CT should be performed to evaluate tibial
plateau fractures because conventional radiographs are not as sensitive in detecting
nondisplaced or minimally displaced fracture lines and smaller areas of articular
impaction. Posteromedial and posterolateral articular fragments and independent tibial
tubercle fragments should be identified and considered in preoperative planning.14,15
Three-dimensional CT reconstruction images may aid in preoperative planning of more
complex fracture patterns (Figure 3). In certain fracture patterns, including fracture-
dislocations, MRI can be performed to assess for injuries to the menisci and ligaments10
(Figure 4).

Fracture Classification

Three classification systems, Schatzker, the AO Foundation/Orthopaedic Trauma Association,
and three-column classification systems, typically are used to describe tibial plateau fractures.
Each classification system describes the fracture, surgical planning, and prognosis.
Schatzker Classification System
The Schatzker classification divides tibial plateau fractures into six different types16 (Figure 5).
Figure 5 Illustrations show the Schatzker classification of tibial plateau fractures. (Reproduced
from Zura R, Kahn M: Fractures of the tibial plateau, in Ricci WM, ed: Orthopaedic Knowledge
Update: Trauma, ed 5. Rosemont, IL. American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2016, pp
533-549.)
Standard AP and lateral radiographs are used to determine the classification type.
The Schatzker types are based on fracture pattern, mechanism of injury, and treatment
approaches.16
AO Foundation/Orthopaedic Trauma Association Classification System
The AO Foundation/Orthopaedic Trauma Association classification system divides tibial
plateau fractures into extra-articular, partial articular, and complete articular (Figure 6).

Subdivisions are based on the degree of comminution.
Three-column Classification System
The three-column classification system was created to address the insufficiencies of other
classification systems in describing sagittal plane fractures.3

This classification system divides the tibial plateau into three columns on an axial CT scan of
the proximal tibia (Figure 7).
Figure 7 Drawing shows the three-column classification of tibial plateau fractures, which
involves the use of an axial CT scan of the knee to compartmentalize fractures in the medial,
lateral, and posterior columns. (Reproduced from Zura R, Kahn M: Fractures of the tibial
plateau, in Ricci WM, ed: Orthopaedic Knowledge Update: Trauma, ed 5. Rosemont, IL. American
Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2016, pp 533-549.)
Treatment Indications
Management of tibial plateau fractures should focus on restoration of knee function to include
painless range of motion without instability.
In deciding between surgical vs nonsurgical management, fracture characteristics and patient
factors should be considered.
Although thresholds for articular incongruity depend on the location of incongruity and patient
age and activity level, any degree of knee instability is poorly tolerated.17

Nonsurgical Management
Similar to any periarticular fracture, progressive early range of motion should be a priority.
Nonsurgical management of tibial plateau fractures should include immobilization via a cast or
brace, followed by progressive knee range of motion for the first 2 to 4 weeks.
Patients should remain non–weight-bearing for 8 to 12 weeks to allow for fracture healing
before progressing to weight bearing as tolerated.
Surgical Management
Goals of surgical management of tibial plateau fracture include anatomic articular reduction,
restoration of condylar width, reestablishment of the coronal and sagittal mechanical axes,
respect for the soft tissues, stable fixation, and early range of motion.
The timing of surgical management and the need for staged, provisional external fixation
depend on the status of the soft tissues and associated injuries.
External Fixation
Longitudinal traction via the pins and bars of a knee-spanning external fixator will provide the
appropriate ligamentotaxis to maintain overall length and alignment.
A simple uniplanar external fixator with four pins placed in a far-far, near-near fashion offers
provisional indirect reduction and stabilization (Figure 8).
Figure 8 Intraoperative photograph of a lower extremity shows external fixation. (Courtesy of
Stephen J. Warner, MD, PhD, Houston, TX.)
Tibial pins should be placed away from the zone of injury and away from the areas of planned
definitive fixation to minimize infection.18

With certain fracture-dislocation patterns, percutaneous manipulation of the femoral and tibial
condyles may be necessary to reduce the knee (Figure 9).
Figure 9 Images of a knee with a tibial plateau fracture-dislocation. Preoperative AP (A) and
lateral (B) radiographs demonstrate the fracture-dislocation. AP (C) and lateral (D) fluoroscopic
images show improved alignment after percutaneous manipulation and external fixation.
(Courtesy of Stephen J. Warner, MD, PhD, Houston, TX.)
Surgical Approaches
Surgical approaches should be determined after careful scrutiny of injury radiographs and CT
scans.
Approaches may need to be altered based on the status of the soft-tissue envelope; any
compromised soft tissue should be avoided if possible (Video 1).
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:34 AM
AAOS | Tibial Plateau Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004097
13/31

Video 1 Kottmeier SA: Proximal tibia, from Jones CB, mod: Surgical exposure trends and
controversies in extremity fracture care. Presented at the Annual Meeting of the American
Academy of Orthopedic Surgeons, Las Vegas, NV, March 12-16, 2019.
Anterolateral Approach
The anterolateral approach is the most common approach used to manage tibial plateau
fractures and is extensile proximally for the lateral femur and distally for the anterolateral
tibia.
It provides access for reduction and fixation of lateral and anterolateral tibial plateau
fractures, including lateral articular depression.
The anterolateral approach is based off location of the Gerdy tubercle and can be a straight, L-
shaped, or S-shaped incision.
A submeniscal arthrotomy often is performed via an anterolateral approach for direct
visualization of the articular surface and for inspection and possible repair of the lateral
meniscus.
Medial Approach
A direct medial or posteromedial approach to the proximal tibia can be used to manage
isolated medial tibial plateau fractures or can be combined with an anterolateral approach to
manage bicondylar tibial plateau fractures.

The posteromedial approach is important for reduction and fixation of posteromedial
fragments and can be performed with the patient in the supine19 or prone3,20 position.
The pes tendons typically are encountered via a medial approach and can be preserved or
tenotomized and repaired if fracture visualization and reduction is impaired.
Posterolateral Approaches
Although not as commonly used as the anterolateral, medial, or posteromedial approaches,
posterolateral approaches may be necessary for specific fracture patterns.
The proximity of posterolateral approaches to the common peroneal nerve and the bifurcation
of the popliteal artery makes surgical access to this area more challenging.
Several types of proximal fibular osteotomies exist to improve access to the posterolateral
tibial plateau.21
Posterior Approaches
The Lobenhoffer approach is useful for managing posteromedial, posterior, and/or
posterolateral fracture components.22
This L-shaped incision extends over the popliteal fossa, and the medial gastrocnemius is
retracted laterally (Figure 10).

A, An L-shaped incision is made over the popliteal fossa. B, The medial gastrocnemius is
retracted laterally. (Courtesy of Stephen J. Warner, MD, PhD, Houston, TX.)
A direct posterior approach can expose the posterior proximal tibia surface and requires
dissection and mobilization of the neurovascular bundle.23
Reduction Techniques
Direct and indirect reduction techniques are useful for the management of tibial plateau
fractures (Video 2).
A universal distractor is valuable for indirect reduction of specific fragments and to provide
joint distraction for improved direct articular visualization (Figure 11).

distractor for indirect reduction of the fragments. C, Lateral fluoroscopic image shows the
application of buttress plates to reduce and stabilize the articular fragments. (Courtesy of

Strategically positioned buttress plates can be used to reduce and stabilize specific articular
fragments (Figure 11).
Articular impaction is best reduced via bone tamps to elevate the associated cancellous and
subchrondral bone (Figure 12).

shows reduction of the lateral tibial plateau with the use of a tamp. B, AP fluoroscopic image
shows application of a lateral plate with the use of a periarticular clamp to compress the
articular surface and reduce the condylar width. AP (C) and lateral (D) radiographs

Periarticular clamps facilitate reduction and restoration of condylar width (Figure 12).

Internal Fixation Techniques
Providing stable fixation to allow for early range of motion is a priority (Video 2).
Implant positions should be planned based on the deformities observed on injury radiographs
and fracture fragments observed on CT scans.
The use of anatomic pre-contoured plates for the proximal tibia may result in malreduction if
the contour is inappropriate for the patient’s anatomy, especially if the plates are used in a
buttress fashion.
Buttress plates for partial articular tibial plateau fragments should be placed over the apex of
the fracture.
After elevation of articular impaction, the residual cancellous void can be filled with the use of
autograft, allograft, or bone graft substitute.24,25
Screws placed in the distal aspects of plates can be placed percutaneously to minimize soft-
tissue dissection and exposure.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:34 AM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004097
18/31

Meniscal tears, which usually are lateral, should be identified and repaired.26
Specific Fracture Patterns
Split-depressed Lateral Tibial Plateau Fractures

Split-depressed Lateral Tibial Plateau Fractures
For Schatzker type II injuries, which are the most common tibial plateau fracture pattern,
CT scans are examined for articular impaction and location of lateral cortical fractures
(Figure 13). Air densities on CT scans highlight the open nature of the injury. An
anterolateral approach is used for exposure. Lateral femur distraction is applied to
induce a varus force across the knee and increase articular exposure via a lateral
submeniscal arthrotomy. A bone tamp is introduced through the lateral cortical fracture
to elevate and reduce the lateral articular surface under direct visualization. Steinmann
pins aid in this reduction, and the residual cancellous defect is filled with the use of
cortical/cancellous allograft. An anterolateral plate is applied and compressed to the
bony surface via a periarticular clamp and cortical screws. Additional cortical screws are
placed proximally to support the articular surface and reduce condylar width.

Bicondylar Tibial Plateau Fractures

Bicondylar Tibial Plateau Fractures
Although bicondylar tibial plateau fractures result in various injury patterns, the most
common pattern includes a relatively simple medial column fracture and a
multifragmentary lateral column fracture with articular depression (Figure 14). The
location of the medial column fracture, including its apex exit point distally, should

dictate the position of medial column fixation for optimal fixation. The medial column
may have multiple fracture fragments and requires multiple plates to ensure stable
fixation (Figure 14). The medial column typically is addressed first because of the simpler
fracture plans and the effect on restoration of the coronal and sagittal planes. A direct
medial, posteromedial, or posterior approach can be performed with the patient in the
supine or prone position, depending on the location of the main medial column
fractures. The medial condyle is reduced and stabilized with the use of appropriately
positioned fixation (Figure 15). Then, the lateral condyle is addressed in a sequence
similar to that for a split-depressed lateral plateau fracture (Figure 15).

AP fluoroscopic image shows reduction with the use of clamps and provisional wire

Posterolateral Tibial Plateau Fractures

Posterolateral Tibial Plateau Fractures
Posterolateral fracture patterns are less common injuries. They may be isolated or
associated with an anterolateral fracture of the medial column. The surgical approach
depends on the location and displacement of the fracture fragments, the status of the
soft tissues and the location of other fracture fragments that need to be addressed. In

9/4/26, 10:34 AM

22/31

patterns with posterolateral and anterolateral components, a Lobenhoffer approach
provides access for reduction and fixation of the posterolateral plateau while allowing
for an adequate skin bridge for an anterolateral approach (Figure 16). Similar to a more
typical bicondylar plateau, reduction and fixation begin with the simpler fracture planes
of the posterolateral plateau and then progress to the comminuted and impacted
anterolateral plateau (Figure 16).
Figure 16 Images of a knee with a multi-fragmentary posterolateral tibial plateau
fracture. Preoperative AP (A) and lateral (B) radiographs demonstrate the nature of the
injury. C and D, Three-dimensional CT reconstruction images show the osseous detail of
the fracture fragments. AP (E) and lateral (F) fluoroscopic images show application of the
posterolateral buttress plates for each fragment. Postoperative AP (G) and lateral (H)
radiographs demonstrate final reduction and fixation. (Courtesy of Stephen J. Warner,
MD, PhD, Houston, TX.)
Tibial Plateau Fractures with an Ipsilateral Tibial Shaft Fracture


Tibial Plateau Fractures with an Ipsilateral Tibial Shaft Fracture
The principles of tibial plateau fracture reduction and fixation should be maintained in
injuries with an ipsilateral tibial shaft. The tibial plateau is reduced first, and initial
fixation should be away from the intended tibial nail path (Figure 17). The posterior
holes of anterolateral proximal tibia plates often are posterior to the pathway of reaming
and nail entry. Clamps should be used to aid in maintaining tibial plateau fracture
reduction during nailing. After nail placement, additional fixation is added to the tibial
plateau.
Figure 17 Images of a knee with a tibial plateau fracture and an ipsilateral tibial shaft
fracture. Preoperative AP (A) and lateral (B) radiographs demonstrate the nature of the

injury. AP (C) and lateral (D) fluoroscopic images show initial reduction and fixation of the
tibial plateau fracture at the start of tibial nailing. E, AP fluoroscopic image shows

Pearls and Pitfalls
Failure to respect the soft tissues may result in a high rate of complications.
Surgical management is indicated to address articular displacement or instability.
Staged management via a provisional external fixator should be performed for fractures with
axial and/or angular instability until the soft tissues are amenable to surgical exposure.
Surgical approaches should be planned according to the relevant fracture fragments and the
soft-tissue envelope.
Posteromedial and posterolateral articular fragments should be recognized for reduction and
stabilization.
Insufficient filling of residual cancellous defect after articular elevation may result in
subsidence and joint incongruity.
Postoperative Management
Patients should be monitored for compartment syndrome in the early postoperative period.
Range of motion with or without a hinged knee brace, which may include continuous passive
motion, should be initiated early.27
Weight bearing is restricted for 6 to 12 weeks, depending on the fracture type.
Complications
Early Complications
The risk of deep surgical site infection after plate fixation of tibial plateau fractures is
approximately 5%.28,29
Infection rates increase to 14% to 24% for bicondylar plateau fractures managed via dual
plating via two approaches.30,31

Temporary external fixation and proper soft-tissue handling may minimize the infection
risk.32,33
Compartment syndrome may occur in 11% to 18% of tibial plateau fractures and correlates
with increased Schatzker type and displacement.30,34
Late Complications
Arthrofibrosis may occur in 15% of patients with a tibial plateau fracture who undergo surgical
treatment, with the use of a provisional external fixator associated with an increased risk.35
Soft-tissue irritation from implants may be prevalent; removal of implants after osseous union
may improve outcomes in these patients.36
Approximately 10% of high-energy bicondylar tibial plateau fractures result in nonunion.30
Posttraumatic arthritis is reported in 30% to 40% of patients after surgical treatment; however,
this radiographic finding does not always correlate with clinical symptoms.37,38
Outcomes
Although functional outcomes after surgical fixation of tibial plateau fractures may be
favorable overall, most patients have midterm to long-term residual dysfunction.38,39
Functional outcomes are correlated with articular reduction and fracture severity.39
Improvements in patient-reported outcomes can be expected as long as 5 years after the
fracture.40
Between 4% and 7% of patients undergo total knee arthroplasty 5 to 10 years after a tibial
plateau fracture, which is influenced by surgeon and hospital volumes.41,42
